This paper presents a time-varying extension of a model first proposed by Davis et al. in 2009, which incorporates time-varying coefficients for both the autoregressive and linking functions. We utilize a generalized linear model framework to develop a temporal varying negative binomial autoregressive model as an alternative. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model estimator.

Unexpectedly, we found that laser-induced aerosol optical depth measurements are accurately predicted using existing stellar photometry technology with high confidence (p=0.1). Conflicting reports on the confidence level were found in a previous meta-analysis.

Langevin dynamics is widely used in molecular simulations for exploring complex free energy landscapes in real-time, particularly in molecular systems with thousands of atoms, due to its efficiency and ability to sample effectively. What sets it apart is the inclusion of a stochastic force, often assumed to be linear and constant, although molecular vibrations often result in non-linear and time-varying effects. This article introduces a sophisticated, non-linear and time-dependent oscillatory external field as an additional force in molecular simulations, allowing for an extended range of sampling molecular configurations without linear response conditions. The field's optimal setting is determined by accepting a high temperature state, although effective free energy landscape exploration is achieved with a non-linear parameter of 0.5 and a temperature of 3000 K in a leucine needle system with a reported free energy barrier of 15.6 kcal/mol between two stable states.

Recent advances in image description generation have sparked interest in using human-provided references to evaluate the quality of generated descriptions. The premise is that human reviewers more readily provide constructive criticism when presented with the original image and any accompanying descriptions. This study investigates the impact of this evaluation method, comparing it to directly assessing generated descriptions. We conducted three experiments with varying descriptions and found that human reference information significantly enhances the accuracy of evaluating generated images description, particularly in experiments with noisy description data.

We present a novel measure of theoretical field intricacy in a geometric context. This context incorporates the intricacy operator, which is defined using concepts from differential geometry. This concept is then linked to an existing polynomial intricacy measure that has already been established in literature. As a foundation, we revisit two intricate equation models, namely the Euler-Arnold and Euler-Poincare-Dark matter models. Subsequently, we define a new intricateity operator within a geometric context and utilize it to investigate the intricateity patterns when applied to various vector fields in a two-dimensional space.

In 1956, Schramm pointed out that there might be some unexplained baryon matter lurking in the universe. Building on this idea, Sato and Cooley expanded the discussion in 1976, suggesting that unexplained baryon deficits could be made up of exotic particles. Here, we present a more detailed analysis, allowing for non-uniform distributions of these particles in the cosmos. When considering a homogeneous distribution, dark baryons could make up to 14% of the dark matter, slightly less if there's a clumped distribution. Notably, if exotic baryons are clustered similarly to ordinary stars, they could account for approximately 2% of the mass within a galaxy's central region, potentially explaining the flat inner regions of its rotation curve.

This article presents SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM-based alternative analyses to our previous research on broadband wireless power and data integration. By leveraging prior findings, we optimize the wireless data rate and power density in a two-time-period, resource allocation scenario. In this model, one period is dedicated to data transmission while the other focuses on OFDM signal processing.

We present a flexible theory framework that allows for the precise adjustment of parton distribution functions (PDFs). This framework is particularly useful in a way that new experimental data can be easily integrated to update existing PDFs. It's shown that both theoretical calculations and experimental data can be expressed in a format that NLLX$-\(n+1\) evolution can be effectively applied. It's been established that the code is capable of adjusting various types of observables, including nested ones, and that it can be used to update PDFs with new data on structure functions $F_1$ and $F_2$. It's also found that data on semi-inclusive deepely virtual scattering can be used in a fashion that's not typically possible and that there are not many differences between updating with combined data sets that include NNNLO calculations and those that don't.

Turbulent fires are prone to instability, causing oscillations that can damage a building's structure. To address this issue, we developed a new numerical model to simulate the interaction between a jet fire, an underlying flexible structure, and sound waves. In this scenario, the model takes into consideration the formation of fire flames through an active flame generation technique. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted a series of tests using highly resolved simulations. In these tests, we observed the effect of varying frequency and intensity levels on the structure of the fire and the resulting vibrations in the underlying platform. Our results showed that flame oscillations induce structural vibrations, which in turn cause additional flame instability through the presence of vortices. To better understand this phenomenon, we conducted linear stability analysis on a flame-synchronized simulation and an idealized steady-state condition, revealing the source of oscillations through an breakdown of the linearized equations. The results of our research provide valuable insights into the interaction between fire, turbulence, and structural dynamics in an attempt to mitigate the risk of resonance in affected buildings.

In nonlocal gravity theory, we reformulate the approach by focusing on two key components: a specific configuration of the Finslerian metric tensor known as the constitutive connection, and a particular setup of the gravitational field that ensures a flat spacetime environment called the essential tetrad.

The LHC on a Half-Millimeter scale is a configuration of the LHC where four batches of procol particles are used to create four distinct events simultaneously, with each event involving a different collision point. In this setup, the batches are used to produce tiny bar-like systems that consist of just a few TeV of energy, with one of the events specifically targeted to create a heavy particle. This paper presents initial results from running this unique configuration, which operates with an integrated luminosity of 250 inverse femtobarns, searching for heavy particles such as top quarks and Higgs bosons. The creation cross sections for these particles in theTiny systems at the LHC ($\epsilon$-LHC) mode are found to be significantly lower than in the conventional mode of operation, with an efficiency of 16% in detecting them, with no heavy particles identified in the Tiny systems ATLAS runs.

Observations of some Galactic Centre X-ray binaries in the past year show increased activity, possibly linked to a pattern noted in these types of binary systems, where bursts of activity occur and then are followed by a period of inactivity, sometimes lasting years. To explain this observed cycle, we propose a model in which a neutron star in an binary system accretes a torus of material after a mass transfer surge, then the system enters a phase where the outflows generated prevent further accretion, before a remnant disk eventually allows the cycle to begin again. Estimating the typical repetition interval of these binary systems by considering the size of the disk and the material's density, we find predicted timescales that generally match what's been observed, with a power law slope of 0.8, varying between 30 and 3000 days, in agreement with recent observations of Galactic Centre X-ray binaries showing activity, and also aligning with data on these types of binary systems deemed dormant in the Milky Way, numbereding around 15 within the Centre, and potentially more on the galactic outskirts, numbereding in the dozens, within the vicinity of the Centre.

Bipartite graphs are a focal point of graph theory, and their structure is characterized by Konigs theorem, which states that they lack odd cycles. A significant open question posed by Erdos and Szekeres establishes a bound on the number of edges in a bipartite graph with $n$ vertices. For smaller graphs, specifically those with a limited number of edges, a structure is identified that allows for an equal partition of vertices, potentially increasing the understanding of bipartite graphs' properties. While this structure is harder to prove, it is evident to know. To further understand the relationship between a bipartite graph's properties and its ability to exhibit a balanced book structure, parameterizing this ability with respect to $k$ is explored. Using Wootton's theorem, which extends Konigs theorem, it is established that a graph satisfying certain conditions, such as an edge limit derived from $n$ and $m$ vertices, will exhibit a balanced book structure of at most two edges. To investigate the efficiency of algorithms in determining this ability, the impact of focusing on smaller graphs with a limited number of edges is explored. In this context, an algorithm is identified that can determine a bipartite graph's partition in a polynomial time, in contrast to a more general result showing that such determination can be challenging for graphs with a significant number of edges. A fundamentally topological method is presented for resolving knots in traditional and welded links, drawing on the concepts of isolated imaginary knittings and modifications.

In dynamic environments, the need for cooperative decisions in multi-robot systems can outpace their available computation and communication capabilities. To address this, we propose a framework where a ensemble of robots work together to make cooperative decisions in a tactical phase, leveraging pre-made plans developed during an strategic phase. We model this decision-making process as a complex collaboration problem, aiming to minimize decision error while minimizing information exchange between robots. We include a centralized solution and a scalable approximate method for this optimization problem, along with theoretical guarantees on its performance. Through various simulation scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms in a stochastic environment.

In our preceding work, we established that the fundamental hyperbolic groups can be incorporated into Garland products of their associated spheres. This paper delves further by providing a more detailed explanation of the proof, focusing on a new approach that utilizes a specific group decomposition. Unlike previous explanations that utilized a product of groups similar to Garland products, our strategy utilizes a configuration of groups arranged in a manner analogous to a torus of groups.

The detection capabilities of interferometric gravitational wave detectors are often constrained by limitations in frequency sensitivity and the response characteristics of the detectors themselves, which are typically mitigated through active or passive resonance enhancement techniques. These methods, however, introduce significant residual noise levels. Resonance sideband techniques, in particular, are limited by the residual noise levels introduced when utilizing high quality factor resonators. The paper proposes an innovative implementation of sideband resonance enhancement within a novel interferometric design called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which features a compact form factor and benefits from a natural linear response to gravitational waves due to its design. The proposed configuration involves a ring of four mirrors, including two suspended at 40 degrees and two fixed, with a laser injected from the center of the ring. The proposed design is analyzed with a quantum-limited model, and a simulated image is produced to demonstrate the effectiveness of sideband cancellation of magnetic noise through resonance sideband techniques within the sloshing Sagnac interferometer design.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems have seen rapid growth, but their potential is hindered by severe inter-user interference, particularly when users are closely grouped. To mitigate this, researchers have explored user distribution strategies that minimize interference by focusing on visible users in non-intersecting service areas. However, current methods often fail to maximize the number of non-intersecting areas and the number of served users. In response, we propose a novel non-intersecting area maximization algorithm specifically designed for XL-MIMO systems. Our algorithm leverages the system's capabilities and involves a initial user segmentation based on XL-MIMO array sectors, a non-intersecting service area optimization based on sector angles, and a user scheduling strategy within each area. Results from simulations show that non-intersecting XL-MIMO service can significantly improve system performance, and our proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of both the number of non-intersecting areas and the total number of served users.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to their superior performance, but we found that neural models' gains may be largely due to their ability to predict high-frequency bigrams, rather than truly understanding language. Our research shows that by pre-training neural models with an $N$-gram loss function that incorporates a residual learning approach, we can significantly enhance both the accuracy and automatic generation capabilities of these models. Specifically, our improved least-squares approach, which addresses issues with gradient vanishing, results in better performance. We observed that modifying the loss function's weighting can further customize the model's generation style, and we observed that our ultimate approach, which combines an $N$-gram loss function with a modified approach, leads to the best performance, which surpasses all previously tried $n$-gram-based models and other standard methods.

This investigation seeks to identify key metrics that are crucial for a system designed to incorporate context from surrounding characters during the recognition of isolated characters, which is typically challenging for optical character recognition systems.

A simplified model of the Earth's atmosphere was used to simulate various wind patterns affected by rotation and temperature differences across the planet's surface in this study and its forthcoming sequel. A three-dimensional anelastic model was employed to investigate the impact of varying the rate of planetary rotation on the emergence of wind patterns in a Mars-like atmosphere with a fixed temperature gradient. A wide range of rotation rates were tested in simulations, spanning two orders of magnitude. The effects of changing the rate of planetary rotation on the development of large-scale circulation patterns were examined by looking at the resulting structures, the most efficient transfer of energy due to differences in rotation and temperature across the planet's surface, as well as the characteristics of turbulent flow.

This study presents an integral reformulation of the reciprocal Gamma function that overcomes traditional regularization requirements, enabling the function to be evaluated at both positive and negative values of $s$.

Following our previous work presented in Ref.1, this study extends our method from non-equilibrium scenarios to equilibrium ones, specifically for Bose fluids. By incorporating a linear potential in conjunction with a sudden change in density, we're able to simulate the formation of a vortex lattice under a linear potential. This research allows us to obtain both the local one-body density matrix and the velocity field, enabling a more in-depth analysis of collective excitations, including zero-point motion, sound waves, and vortex lattice dynamics. Furthermore, we're in a position to calculate the spectral function and the Euler pressure, facilitating the verification of the quantum hydrodynamic approach's ability to accurately depict the many-body equilibrium state of a weakly interacting Bose fluid.

We provide an overview of two advanced optimization techniques: Entropic Regularized Message Passing (ERMP) and Mean-Variances Regularized Message Passing (MVMP). This summary enables our previous work to present fully constructive proofs of their efficiency in accelerating Find the Optimal Threshold in Markov Random Games.

This article establishes that the stabilizer $R_n$ actually generalizes the Racah algebra, which is known as $C_2^{\text{rec}}(n)$ for $n=2$. This generalization holds true for specific values of $n$ and is applicable in the context of polynomial specialization. Furthermore, this article proves that a specialized version of the $\\mathfrak{sl}_2$'s multiplication operation within the quotient of the stabilizer $R_4$ leads to a structure equivalent to the higher rank Wedderburn algebra $W_3$. This equivalence contributes to resolving a mathematical conjecture posed by O'Brien et al. Paired-tests serve as a reliable evaluation method for assessing a permutation operator's effectiveness in comparing a model's output with another permutation outcome. Among available paired-tests, we focus on two structured tests, paired-permutation and paired-Per-Position Permutation tests, along with their variations, for more meaningful assessments. We devise new algorithms to streamline the paired-permutation test, eliminating redundant checks, and present an end-to-end algorithm for the paired-Per-Position Permutation test. Our experimental results using name-matching, OBAMA test data, and a large-scale automated test data set demonstrate the efficacy of these three tests in accurately ranking high-quality paired decision-making algorithms.

Following the characteristics observed in experimental data, we have extended the application of the PMDN theoretical framework to study heavy ion collisions, specifically Cu+Cu and Au+Au, at an energy level of 200 GeV. In this study, we have examined the outcomes of these collisions across a range of centralities, after which we have analyzed the resulting particle distributions, including elliptical and triangular flow coefficients ($n=2,3$), in relation to centralities. Our results indicate that the PMDN model effectively reproduces the experimental observations of $v_2$ and $v_2/N_{\rm part}$ in both Cu+Cu and Au+Au collisions. Furthermore, we have observed that the initial asymmetry in the interaction point contributes to an increase in triangular flow ($v_3$) as centralities become more peripheral.

This paper presents a predictive filter suitable for multi-target tracking applications, characterized by a lattice-based birth model where birth probabilities are confined to a lattice structure, and new targets emerge on lattice points. A streamlined algorithm is introduced to compute the density at lattice points, while an exact method is proposed to calculate the integral required for points outside the lattice. Leveraging this algorithm, the research explores the optimization of sensor resources in a system with multiple targets and a finite number of sensors, with the aim of maximizing detection probability under a bandwidth limit. The proposed method is extended to incorporate additional lattice-based actions, such as prioritizing targets or guiding a guide, in a more complex scenario.

The dynamic nature of soccer makes determining the most effective action to score at any given moment during a game a complex task. To address this, we propose a novel decision support system that utilizes a large-scale, highly detailed soccer data set from German Bundesliga league games, comprising 1046 games and over 250,000 moments, to predict the optimal penalty kick strategy and team movement strategy in corner kick situations. We have designed specific state representations and defined several reward functions for these strategy problems, employing a variable-size convolutional neural network for moment data processing. To incentivize learning, we defined multiple reward functions, including angle-based and variance-based penalties for perceived risky actions, along with incentives for high-value moments. Utilizing a Hierarchy of Action Space and Value Function with varying weights for angle and variance considerations through Appex-1 algorithm, we were able to derive the best strategy in each situation through deep reinforcement learning. To evaluate our corner kick and non-penalty kick models, we conducted specific tests and conducted comparative analyses with baseline strategies, demonstrating the effectiveness of our learned strategies through simulated scenarios. Specifically, our optimal penalty kick strategy outperformed the 50 percent default strategy in terms of scoring probability, and our corner kick model's proposed strategy also showed improvement over static and random strategies. To further validate the practicality and real-game relevance of our corner kick strategy, we analyzed 114 real corner kick situations from Bundesliga league games.

The paper addresses the challenge of obtaining two-dimensional measurements using a single-point laser Doppler anemometer (LDV) system. By employing a controller located far from the measurement area, we successfully implement three-dimensional particle tracking within the sample's light intersection zone. This setup results in high-resolution velocity spectra with minimal signal loss compared to conventional LDV systems. The proposed method's advantage lies in its ability to achieve precise measurements without the complexity and costs associated with large-scale systems, making it particularly beneficial for applications in confined spaces and unconventional geometries.

We provide explicit expressions for the operators constituting the Klein-Gordon equation anharmonic oscillator system in terms of creation and annihilation operators. By leveraging this factorization, we establish the system's linear equivalence to two uncoupled equations in this context. Building on this result, we proceed to analyze the spectral and orbital stability of this system by exploiting existing theories. We highlight the connection between this context and the Nelson model, noting its relevance in quantum field theory context.

In hadron decays, particularly those of heavy particles like $D$ and $B$, the axion-like particle (ALP) search space is divided into two distinct areas: decays occurring near the primary collision point and those occurring in a displaced location. To effectively use Belle II data in searching for $B$ decays into an electron or muon and an ALP, which may then decay into two photons, we propose two different Belle II subdetectors that can capture this rare occurrence. An additional, hypothetical subdetector is described, capable of detecting an ALP that does not decay within a given volume, resulting in a signature of a missing energy particle.

This study investigates the levels of effectiveness and the underlying mechanisms of contextualized language models in identifying changes in meaning during text editing. We investigated the model's performance by modifying the semantics, syntax, or both in the documents it processed. We evaluated the performance of three contextualized language models: Average, Syntax-Aware, and Semantics-Aired, based on how often they successfully detected modifications in a modified documents. Our results showed that modifying the syntax or the semantics of the documents processed led to variations in the documents' labels assigned by the models, according to a one-way ANOVA test. We created and used more in-depth modifications to the documents processed to help restore the documents' labels as the model learned or the documents processed, based on a multiple ANOVA analysis. We used various analyses, including modifying specific words and phrases in the documents processed, to help reveal the mechanism by which the models learned to identify alterations in syntax or semantics. Our findings indicated that the models relied on maintaining the documents' syntax and semantics to help assign the documents processed their initial labels. We used various modifications to the initial training data sets the model used to help demonstrate that the model learned the documents processed initial syntax and semantics as well as the modifications in meaning associated with them.

A active galactic nucleus (AGN) consists of a massive central black hole that may be surrounded by a disk of accreting matter and produce a jet. Because the behavior of the material around the black hole is independent of the physics of gravitational waves, spin measurement can provide initial information about the source's behavior, making it useful for gravitational wave detection. A recent study has filled a gap in the analysis of active galactic nuclei by investigating the interaction between a black hole and a giant gas cloud, which can affect the black hole's velocity and ultimately lead to gravitational wave emission. Because a giant gas cloud is required for this process, it is considered rare, and a larger sample of relevant data is needed to draw more robust conclusions. A theoretical model has been developed to determine the rate at which a black hole and a boson interact, taking into account the spin of the black hole and the size and density of the boson, which can then be integrated to derive a halo mass limit given a specific distribution of black hole spins. A analysis of data from the PaO and PARAMETRIZED models has revealed that a uniform halo of certain types of bosons is inconsistent with the observed spin values of a large number of massive black holes, yielding 90% confidence confidence intervals of less than $10^{-12} GeV$ for a scalar and $10^{-10}$ eV for a vector particle. This study formulates a non-equilibrium scenario for a quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to constant forces applied at its ends, initiating it in an excited state.

Introducing a novel variation of traditional hyperproperties, our work defines a new type of hyperproperty termed a quantum relational pre-property. This new pre-property type facilitates the formulation of a quantum relational variant of the Hoare logic framework, ideal for establishing correctness proofs of quantum algorithms. The resulting relational quantum hoare logic framework extends conventional hyperproperty-based correctness models, and the authors specifically introduce two quantum relational specifiers, contextual and contextual+, to enable the proof of algorithmic correctness when dealing with multiple input and output quantum states. The contextual+ specifier in particular is specifically tailored to support proof of correctness for quantum error correction codes, code replication for enhanced error tolerance, and amplitude estimation algorithms.

The paper addresses the problem of polarization signal bias that leads to inaccurate reconstructions of magnetic fields in the solar surface, particularly in areas with strong magnetic fields. This issue is seen in measurements considered vector magnetic field outputs and is discussed in detail along with its sources. One method to counter this bias by obtaining more accurate magnetic field estimates from polarization signal data is also presented.
Lattice theory is explored through a graph structure defined by specific relations $s_1$ and $s_2$ within the set of involutions on a boolean lattice $B_n$.

This research paper examines two curved paths in a three-dimensional, unit-sized Lorentzian manifold and confirms that specific conditions outlined in two theorems by the following authors constitute Timelike Bertrand Curves: the first described by Napoleon points from a triangle as outlined in Article 1, and the second defined on a hyperbola as outlined in Article 2.

This paper aims to ALN a concept introduced earlier, which enables researchers to investigate the role of loss function design in a specific machine learning system. Our initial exploration, conducted on three distinct data sets, yields inconclusive results. Consequently, we set out to evaluate loss function designs from a broader perspective by assessing ten specific configurations on four data sets. Our comprehensive analysis, involving both quantitative and qualitative assessments, yielded surprising findings. Notably, we observed that the loss function design has a substantial impact on data sets with intricate structures or a data imbalance, such in ARA-VO data set. However, its influence is negligible data sets with well-established performance benchmarks, such as CIFAR-10. Furthermore, we discovered that certain loss function designs that typically underperform in standard machine learning tasks can yield beneficial results in situations characterized by data imbalance.

This paper introduces an comprehensive repository of cross-domain machine common knowledge consisting of 144 inferred rules derived from 17 diverse datasets within the OSTEST framework. What sets our work apart is its focus on structured inference relationships such as AND, OR, and IMPLIES, filling the gap left by most existing studies that are limited to independent OSTEST dataset evaluations. By utilizing individual data points to verify OSTEST scenarios, we enable sophisticated if-then inference capabilities in a zero-shot setting. Our contributions culminate in the largest structured machine common knowledge atlas to date, catalyzing subsequent research and practical applications.

To improve video forecasting, this research has developed a unique approach that considers both the semantic content and motion of videos. The method utilizes a dual representation that considers graph-based and Euclidean-based features to capture the temporal, semantic, and complex patterns of videos. A novel hybrid model is proposed to predict the future states of a video. Results from multiple experiments show that this approach outperforms existing methods.

A finite graph's "metric dimension" is a concept that's been studied for over five decades, but a related idea, which we've coined as the "shortened metric dimension," has not been explored until now. In this paper, we introduce the "shortened metric dimension" as a variant of the original concept, where a resolving set may leave some graph vertices with unresolved ambiguities, but aims to minimize the total residual distance between such vertices. This is a helpful attribute that could have various applications, one of which we've identified as a graph's identification number used in networking protocols. Following we provide mathematical characterizations of both the "shortened metric dimension" and its derived parameter, the "shortened DM value" for finite graphs, along with formulas to calculate their respective average values across all possible finite graphs.

This study aims to classify heart sounds into five categories: normal heart sound and five types of murmurs (CICD, QRD, QRDE, SIM, SIMC) as defined by the American Heart Association. A unique dataset has been constructed through computer-generated defective models and CICD simulations, with cyclic defective models created using Finite Element Method and defective models generated via Quadratic Reforming techniques. A combination of MPE cyclic technology, Quadratic Reforming models, and simulated sound data produced the training material. A Deep Learning model, consisting of a CNN backbone followed by an BLSTM layer and a fully connected classifier, achieved the best classification results with 87.3% accuracy.

We examined the emission of the fine structure lines of neutral atomic iodine (77$\mu$m and 1282$\mu$m) in galaxies and found the energy input required to produce these lines is insufficient to excite hydrogen recombination lines observed in galaxies. This indicates a non-thermal mechanism is responsible for these emissions. A number of structural features within galaxies, including outer regions, discs, and peripheral rings, are likely sites where this non-thermal mechanism occurs. Its potential drivers, such as gravitational shear, spiral arm structures, and stellar birth events, are numerous. The discovery is noteworthy as it reveals a previously unrecognized channel for stellar formation in galaxies and suggests a hitherto unknown component of dust heating in molecular gas clouds. A variety of structural features within galaxies are likely sites where this subthermal stimulation takes place, and its causes are numerous, including spiral arm structures, gas accretion, tidal interactions, and turbulence.

boundaries. This dynamic approach, which gradually alters the asymmetry
parameter (velocity) of the model, enables the system to reach an
equilibrated state in a non-equilibrium setting. By examining this
specific scenario, an exact expression has been derived for the steady-state
current flowing through the system in its steady state.

The global COVID-19 pandemic has spurred a surge in epidemiological research, particularly in mathematical modeling. As the epidemic progresses, an extensive array of models has been developed, posing a challenge in navigating the vast literature for both researchers and policymakers. This paper presents a review of mathematical models' key aspects, their limitations, strengths, and appropriate contexts for outlining the dynamics of infectious disease outbreaks. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the models' relevance by outlining how they can be used to track outbreak trends, with a focus on recent studies analyzing the COVID-19 situation in a specific region.

This multi-task learning approach addresses the challenge of determining feelings in English and Arabic content, utilizing both labeled and unabeled data. Labeled data consists of bilingual sentiment information, while unabeled data involves applying domain adaptation techniques to enhance accuracy.

Recently, major online platforms have experienced a surge in the distribution of fake news through manipulated multimedia content, posing a significant challenge due to the vast amount of data and the complexity of the problem. In an effort to tackle this issue, we construct a unique dataset named UMN-SC, which comprises 160,000 news articles accompanied by images and is annotated based on the political polarized topic of the 2020 US-South China Sea incident. Following the data pre-processing, we devise a novel model called Meta-PMC, which utilizes meta-learning to detect fake news through a shared knowledge representation that integrates text and image data. In our model, a metalearner learns to quickly adapt features using neural process networks, which are employed to generate a dynamic weight matrix for the attention mechanism of the LSTM network. The results obtained from our experiments demonstrate that the Meta-PMC model outperforms existing methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. Furthermore, ablation experiments provide additional insights into the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

This paper presents the design of Golay complementary structures applicable to multi-stage frequency division multiple access systems. Initially, we provide concise overviews of both single and multiple pair Golay complementary sequences, highlighting recent advancements. Subsequently, we systematically document multiple design methods, including constructive approaches, algebraic techniques, and recursive strategies for generating structures with zero auto-correlation in multiple stages.

This research introduces a method for creating trained medical image datasets that have had specific areas damaged in the brain simulated within them, as training is found to be necessary for the model to produce realistic lesions, as it is discovered to be critical for effective treatment planning.
提出一种名为 CAE，即对比学习的网络模型，旨在从广泛的文本资料中提取特定属性。 CAE 包含两个主要模块：一个用于整合不同描述方式的文本匹配结构，另一个用于处理缺失属性的推断结构。通过对比不同属性，该模型能提升整体性能。为证实 CAE 的优越性，我们在十个大型电商产品的数据集上进行测试，结果表明其表现优于现有的网络模型。

Recent advances in training extensive language models have produced high-performing models. While efficiency-focused techniques have led to cost-effective solutions, these models often lack in depth on complex tasks such as reasoning about logic and mathematics problems. Our proposed method, which is a sophisticated approach designed to enhance the capabilities of large language models, focuses on teaching them intricate concepts similar to deductive reasoning through additional training. We've developed an automated system, consisting of around 13k distinct problems with varying structures and rules to use in these training sessions, which has proven effective in teaching large language models these intricate concepts. Our findings demonstrate that the model, even when reduced in size to 6 or 13 parameters, shows significant improvement in its ability to reason about logical problems, whether the rules involve ranking, sorting, or various other structures, surpassing other enhanced large language models and even untrained models with larger vocabularies. Additionally, the model, which has been specifically trained to reason about logical problems, demonstrates an improved understanding of the importance of transitivity and other related concepts.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics when particle pairs are produced in highly intense fields. This nonlinearity results in a new effect called as non-linear charge, which can influence the behavior of black holes by modifying the interaction between them and the surrounding geometry. Non-linear charge quantifies the impact of this effect and is a function of the black hole's properties, including its mass, charge, and the Adamowski parameter. A linear approximation is commonly used to estimate a black hole's charge, but a more accurate approach involves solving a cubic equation to determine the equivalent non-linear charge. A key finding of our study is that both linear and non-linear charges produce similar results under certain conditions, but diverge under others, particularly when an Adams-like parameter is highly positive. A phase diagram is developed to illustrate the impact of non-linear charge, linear charge, linearity parameter, and Adamowski parameter on black hole behavior. A novel concept called shadow thermodynamics is proposed to describe the pattern of extremal, naked singularities, and horizonless black holes and is found to align with the Erromano-Ruiz-Castro diagram. A critical line is identified to illustrate the connection between non-linear charge and shadow thermodynamics. A key discovery is made showing that a cubic phase diagram of an black hole shadow radius is analogous to a magnetic field phase diagram of iron.

Following the principles of quantum information theory, our research demonstrates the transformation of a specific non-linear interaction involving two harmonic oscillators into a correlated state of velocities, and in a more non-classical scenario into a synchronized oscillation through continuous variable teleportation protocols.

Following the identification of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_C$ mode, we have now analyzed additional data to search for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ transition, yielding no significant results. Based on a combined dataset corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 3.0 inverse terabarns at center-of-mass energies of 13 and 13.6 TeV, no significant signal was observed for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ transition, setting a upper limit of $19\times10^{-8}$, and for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ transition, yielding no significant results, resulting in an upper limit of $100\times10^{-8}$.

A module $M$ can be viewed as a representation of an algebra $\mathcal{A}$, resulting in a vector space with a vector space representation of $\mathcal{A}$. Consequently, vector submodules of $M$ can be regarded as subspaces that represent the algebra through submodules, essentially functioning as subspaces of the vector space. Previously, an effective method was introduced to construct the lattice of vector submodules of $M$ from the lattice of submodules of $M$ in relation to an ideal $\mathcal{I}$ of the algebra $\mathcal{A}$, in cases where the submodules of $\mathcal{M}$ that are not composed of the vector space representation are easily identifiable and the lattice of submodules regarding $\mathcal{I}$ is known. This article expands upon that approach, constructing the lattice of vector submodules of $M$ from the lattice of submodules of $M$ in relation to an ideal $\mathcal{I}$ of the algebra $\\mathcal{A}$, under slightly modified conditions.
We explore how several operators including curvature collineation, concyclic concurrence, and similar operators act in specific types of hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space.

In our study, we developed an efficient algorithm to resolve a longstanding open problem posed by Fraencony and Gyenge, proving that any collection of integers where the ratio of any pair is a rational number p/q forms an ideal code. Our approach relies on a recursive strategy to find a subset comprising elements whose mutual ratios are unique.

Following recent measurements of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ decay by both the LHCb and Belle experiments, the Particle Data Group has updated the function form used to describe this semi-leptonic transition form factor. This specific decay is well-suited for polarized spin-tagging of $B_s^0$ mesons, enabling the measurement of asymmetry in spin-0 and spin-1 $B_{s}^{0}$ decays. To better understand the physics involved, we analyze the connection between this decay mode's angular distribution and charged particle asymmetries, and calculate the relevant form factor shape from first principles using Operator Product Expansion techniques. This calculation focuses on the energy range of the $D_s^{*-}$ meson, revealing that tree-level current algbera relations account for most of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\nu_{\mu}+\mu^{+}$ decay amplitude.

When a material fracture occurs, it can generate acoustic emissions that are sometimes correlated with one another in a concealed manner. We reveal a previously unrecognized, multi-tiered pattern of spatial correlation in a specific fracture process: a sticky tape being removed from a acoustically active bilayer material configuration. In this particular setup, we observe a cluster of audible cracks tied to a specific tangent angle of removal, whereas simulations indicate that symmetric, bipartite distribution of detachment points would result in uncoupled monopole acoustic sources. This implies that the observed, tiered pattern of correlation originates from a more complex, multi-tiered arrangement of simultaneous fractures. We further support our findings through random cluster analysis and numerical simulations.

Geometric structures derived from angle space relations, where the connection exists between pairs of segments sharing a common endpoint if their corresponding angles satisfy a specific order, have been examined. This study presents a new geometric structure that satisfies all conditions proposed by Menger in 1916 and 1928, demonstrating that these angle relations do not fully constitute a partial order. Additionally, it disproves two conjectures by Menger with an example, before providing a constructive proof of the existence of this new geometric structure, and discussing its significance.

Point cloud data often suffers from issues related to coordinate system origins and rotational alignment, which can hinder their effective analysis. To address these issues, researchers have developed smoothening methods that ensure consistent feature extraction regardless of rotational discrepancies. However, these approaches often fall short in capturing features related to point cloud translations. Our proposed approach, Transformation-Dependent Smoothening (TPC), overcomes this limitation by addressing both rotational and translational discrepancies. The core idea involves decomposing spherical feature spaces into discrete sections to address translational issues subsequent to smoothing point cloud data. We identify the optimal smoothening threshold that retains the most informative spherical features, and we determine the ideal threshold value specific to each situation. Our analysis reveals that the (1,-1) grid resolution works best for most situations. Experimental results on three common point cloud classification tasks, including model fusion outcomes, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, particularly in tackling difficult classification tasks.

The structural framework of a type system combined with the operational dynamics of a programming language enable a program verification method known as geometric program checking. This verification approach allows for the visualization of programs and their verification records as geometric shapes, where checking equiva- lence transforms into a geometric problem of aligning shapes. This concept is particularly effective in functional programming languages, demonstrating how simple and robust verification can be achieved without complicated setups. This visual- ization is especially beneficial for understanding and confirming functional exten- sions such as recursive definitions, algebraic data types, pattern matching, record structures, and variation.

To improve the accuracy of mapping electrical properties in heterogeneous composite materials with contrasting conductivity levels, a new computational strategy has been developed. This harmonic-based contouring method utilizes simulated annealing evolutionary algorithms to precisely determine the interface shape that creates a specific harmonic response, corresponding to various electrode configurations. This method's success in finding unique or multiple solutions is demonstrated through a set of simulated tests in rectangular composite samples, revealing precise interface mapping capabilities under specific harmonic responses.

We develop a tensor theory within a finite-dimensional vector space that aligns with geometric intuition, leveraging exterior algebra and a polynomial algebra of a vector. This approach eliminates the need for index notation and cumbersome computations, streamlining calculations into basic vector operations like addition, subtraction, cross product, and expansion along normal vectors. This method is particularly advantageous in understanding the physics and geometry of the resulting (2,0)-tensors, which are viewed as linear operators, and is well-suited for instructional purposes.

A right-angled Artin group (RAAG) associated with a graph G can be viewed as the free group of its collection of unique cycles through a free generating set. It is possible to define a new graph D that describes the invariant relations between these cycles. In our work, we delineate a collection of equivalence relations on this group that results in a hierarchy of groups linked by specific actions, all of which are also right-angled Artin groups. This new graph that describes the relationships between these groups is shown to be isomorphic to the initial graph G.

Recent advances in iterative matrix inversion methods on GPUs have led to improvements reducing iteration counts. We introduce enhancements to an existing method, allowing users to pre-process a symmetric positive-definite matrix to enable larger updates in iterative inversion processes directly on GPUs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique through numerical experiments.

Situational linear bandits is a more complex variant of the classical linear bandit problem, where a client makes a decision in a specific context that directly impacts a particular outcome. In this problem setup, there exists a diverse array of possible contexts, and the client only learns about the repercussions of their chosen action after a short period of time. To enhance their understanding of how their decisions affect outcomes, the client can engage with an external entity, referred to as a learner, who can offer a new context to explore. This paper focuses on a distributed version of this problem, where the client and the learner operate independently, and the learner aims to minimize the negative impact of decisions that yield poor outcomes. To achieve this objective, the client engages in a simple context-sharing activity with the learner, and this paper presents a straightforward strategy for the learner that guarantees a significant reduction in the negative impact of decisions that yield poor outcomes, and a simple example illustrating the limitations of this sharing activity.

A phenomenon observed in protoplanetary disk edges is what led us to investigate the interaction between growth of dust particles and wind speeds causing instability from shear. Initially, we considered a theoretical disk model that we then modified to mimic dust settling, where we modified the viscosity and vantage point of the simulator. As we made more massive and flatter disks, we found that gravitational instability would form closer to the disk's center. As we settled disks further, we discovered that instability was harder to sustain. We then moved to a three-dimensional disk model that we modified to better mimic dust settling in disks of varying mass. In these models, we found that growth of vertical layers resulted in a decoupling of the disk's surface and mid-layer, making the solar system more susceptible to instability. We then created a layered disk model that we modified to mimic a central accretion of dust, finding that as we created distinct layers, we found that instability was harder to sustain. Based on our findings, we concluded that gravitational instability and dust settlement are interconnected, and that larger particles may help create instability in low-mass disk edges.

This paper proves a theorem on differential geometry called a Liouville theorem for bounded solutions of a Ricci curvature equation with constant scalar curvature. The proof relies on geometric analysis techniques. The paper's results have significant implications, particularly in understanding the curvature properties of complete Riemannian manifolds.

This paper presents a new architecture for creating gender-identifying
COCO dataset subset images with high accuracy, incorporating gender
classification capabilities into a Gender-Removed Model without degrading its
accuracy in Gendervitration tasks. By integrating gender classification into
a Gendervitless Model, our approach achieves significant improvements over
existing gender-agnostic methods, with the top three ranked models showing
gender classification accuracy gains of 2.7%, 4.2%, and 5.0% across linear,
gradual, and sudden voice pattern changes respectively, without compromising
visual task performance.

The integration of heterogeneous data in federated learning systems presents a substantial obstacle. This issue is exacerbated when model updates are standardized across clients, as the complexities of data variations can be further compounded. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel model customization technique that incorporates a random walk strategy, designed to mitigate data biases in a federated learning environment without requiring an explicit graph structure. This algorithm is particularly well-suited for federated learning in education systems, where it can effectively leverage visual information to infer a student's knowledge state at each update step. Our proposed method, VV-SDG-MLP, demonstrates its viability through a range of experiments conducted on visual recognition and language learning tasks, consistently delivering satisfactory outcomes in these contexts.

This paper explores a simple and effective consistency regularization method, implemented using AWK, to enhance the performance of deep learning models in the task of medical image segmentation. Although this new technique may appear unconventional due to its use of AWK, a programming language often considered basic and underutilized in scientific research, it produces significant improvements in segmentation accuracy measured by Dice Coefficient scores. A comparative analysis with existing consistency regularization methods implemented using Python reveals that this AWK-based approach outperforms established methods, demonstrating its effectiveness despite utilizing a programming language often overlooked in scientific research.

We resolve a longstanding debate surrounding the interpretation of single-particle entanglement, which has been described as a paradox by some, such as Einstein, and a real phenomenon by others, including Bohr. To clarify this issue we present a formal definition of single-particle entanglement as a specific arrangement where a quantum state is influenced by nonlocal projections operated in distinct regions of space, a configuration that mirrors subjectivespaciality. We further identify this state configuration with the single-particle guidance principle, a concept put forward by Bohr, which demonstrates its fundamental nature by illustrating how nonlocal projections in separate regions can be used to nonlocally manipulate a nondegenerate sharp property of the particle. To establish the genuine quantum mechanical significance of this nonlocal manipulation we derive a version of the violation of local hidden variable theories for single-particle interference patterns.

The integration of Information and Communication Technologies in vehicular systems has gave rise to sophisticated applications, sparking intense competition for limited radio resources and data privacy concerns. These challenges have led to the proposal of federated learning in Internet of Vehicles systems, though its specific implementation details have not been thoroughly explored. This research fills that gap by outlining a framework for privacy-preserving educational systems that uphold data confidentiality and adapt to the dynamic nature of IoVs environments. Key technologies such as blockchain and federated learning are examined in detail, along with protocol designs, incentive mechanisms, and system architectures. Potential directions for upcoming research are also discussed.

Neural network architectures like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) offer powerful video identification capabilities but their practical use is hindered by computational intensity and large size. In contrast, Tensor Decomposition techniques such as Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition are more efficient and compact, although they may lose some neural network capabilities. This paper presents an advanced combined neural-Tensor model called HD-LSTM and an energy-efficient hardware design featuring an LSTM processor and decomposer on a single chip. The HD-LSTM design optimizes the neural network by reducing its dimensions without sacrificing performance, and the hardware design further improves efficiency by skipping unnecessary computations and sharing resources. Evaluations show that both the HD-LSTM design and hardware design significantly lower memory usage and power consumption while maintaining high identification accuracy.

This paper examines solutions to the Schrödinger equation outside a convex obstacle, where the equation features a focusing nonlinearity that decreases with distance raised to a power Omega greater than two. We consider the case where nonlinearity is inactive inside the obstacle and determine conditions for solutions that "explode" in a finite time. By utilizing a specific choice of initial data, we establish the existence of such explosive solutions. Conversely, we utilize an variance identity introduced by Varvaruca and Viola to prove that solutions remain glob ally stable if the initial data is below a specific threshold related to the first eigenvalue of the Neumann Laplacian inside the obstacle.

Following the notation of D. Panov, this article provides proofs for two main results, Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, which replace previously stated conjectures. Specifically, we provide a semi-parametric local abbreviation local uniform scheme for varieties over polynomial rings in positive characteristic, reducing the number of generators by at most one, and a similar result for local rings of algebraic varieties in positive characteristic, also reducing the number of generators by at most one. Notably, these results differ from a similar theorem in characteristic zero, as demonstrated by a counter-example derived from a counter-example by Cox, Little, and Schenck, showing that a certain variety over a two-dimensional polynomial ring in characteristic two requires a local ring with more than a certain number of generators as it stands.

Bayes factors, a tool for evidence-based decision making in model selection, have several advantages but also face significant hurdles. While they offer an objective method for model comparison that avoids some pitfalls of prior sensitivity, their computation can be computationally demanding, particularly when dealing with complex nested models. Additionally, the interpretation of their numerical values lacks a consensus, necessitating the development of a shared language and understanding of their scale. To address these issues, we propose a three-stage framework for leveraging Bayes factors effectively. This initial phase involves evaluating candidate models through descriptive statistics and graphical representations to eliminate poor-fitting options. The second phase leverages Bayes factors to distinguish between remaining viable models, with the option to refine the analysis by updating models if necessary. The final phase consists of presenting the selected best-fitting model, with the Bayes factor incorporated into the description to justify the choice. By integrating descriptive statistics, graphical displays, and Bayes factors in this framework, we aim to enhance the reliability of inferences drawn during the model selection process.

The significance of discourse indicators in NLP has been amplified recently, particularly in relation to neural network models. Despite their purported importance, there's a gap as existing taxonomies lack sufficient semantic annotations and meaningful labels, hindering analysis and research efforts. To address this, we've created a comprehensive, semantically annotated discourse indicator taxonomy consisting of 314 distinct labels, categorized into 15 groups. Our in-depth study involved testing 3112 discourse indicators using 104 evaluation metrics, revealing the necessity of context-specific model training for effective discourse indicator identification. Additionally, we've curated a high-quality dataset of 5800 indicators, validated by human judgment, to facilitate future research. Our proposed approach, dubbed DiscSense, outperformed existing models in our evaluation, underscoring the intricate nature of discourse indicator classification.

A specific deformation of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\lambda)$, known as the Jordanian twist, has led to a modified quantum product and complex conjugate product. This article aims to expand upon the previous results by explicitly calculating the modified complex conjugate and star operations, as well as a vast collection of rational functions belonging to the quantum plane.

This article algorithmizes comparing two regular expressions, A and B, based on their language lengths where $L(\bar{a})$ represents the language matched by regular expression A and $|w|$ denotes the character count of string $w$. An example of comparing two regular expressions is given, such as checking if $|正则表达式1| < |正则表达式2|$ to prioritize search results in a database based on description length. Algorithms used for calculating and comparing the lengths of regular expressions, which are more accurate and efficient than existing methods, are also explained.

In the context of a 2D conformal field theory, we explicitly compute the conformal block for a three-point correlation function involving two primary operators in motion and a composite operator generated by their interaction, when considered in global and rotating coordinates. By switching to light-cone coordinates on the boundary, this computation in global and rotating coordinates reduces to the standard Rota-tion conformal block computation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in both coordinate systems, the three-point correlation function computation is equivalent to a specific limit of the AdS$_3$ three-point correlation function, computed using hyperbolic coordinates.

To expand the field of view (FOV) that lobster-eye lenses can cover, we have investigated and proposed a novel configuration in which multiple lenses are arranged in a multi-layered setup. While previous studies have shown that a single lobster-eye lens has a limited FOV of about 100 degrees due to particle reflection limitations, this multi-layered concept shows promise in significantly increasing the FOV through the use of multiple layers. Simulation results obtained from Geant4 demonstrate that a three-layered setup can achieve a FOV of over 300 degrees with minimal performance loss in terms of detection efficiency.

Interferometric atomic sensors capable of detecting minute variations in local magnetic fields hold immense potential for enhancing fundamental physics research and advancing quantum-enabled geospatial technology. To accomplish this, a sophisticated experimental setup was designed that expands the sensing range of atomic interferometers through the utilization of field variations induced by a superconductor's Meissner effect. In this arrangement, an atomic wave packet is subject to two separate momentum states induced by two successive 2-pi Sagnac effects, creating a broad coherence area stretched over a substantial distance. Consequently, even slight displacements of the superconducting material evoke pronounced local magnetic field changes that impact the atomic interference patterns. Through the utilization of this configuration, researchers were able to detect minute local magnetic field variations through interference patterns, demonstrating the feasibility of utilizing the Meissner effect to amplify minuscule magnetic Sagnac effects. As a result, this innovative design allows for direct measurement of local magnetic field alterations through local interference patterns, achieving a sensitivity of 0.5 nRad/s2 in a specific experiment. Moreover, this setup is anticipated to further enhance sensitivity through the utilization of larger coherence areas, superconducting structures of varying shapes and sizes, and more intricate patterns of interference achieved through multiple interference loops.

During its formulation, the theoretical framework of Yu--Rusinov (YR) states relies on a dirty superconducting gap that exhibits a finite finite density of states at the Fermi energy. This characteristic contradicts the fundamental tenets of superconductivity. This paper proposes a fresh perspective on YR states that aligns with basic superconducting ideals and is applicable to a magnetic impurity on a superconducting surface. According to this principle-based relativistic initial framework, YR states actually manifest as induced magnetic moments that arise due to the splitting of superconducting bound states, resulting in distinct spin-up and spin-down energy levels.

This paper presents a deep learning-based classifier, an auto-encatcher derived model, to assist in distinguishing between benign and malignant skin lesions for diagnostic purposes. Following successful results on image classification tasks, dermatological images were utilized for the research, obtained from two established datasets, SKGV1 and FGVC7. The FGVC7 dataset was found to be particularly valuable due to its larger sample size of 5,000 images, in contrast to the SKGV1 dataset which comprised 1,000 images. The efficacy of the proposed methods was validated through rigorous testing, demonstrating superior performance compared to other deep learning-based approaches. Notably, the FGVC7 dataset's reliability was confirmed through the removal of outlier images, further validating their utility for medical research purposes.

In the context of high-energy muon neutrino interactions, we present a novel approach that leverages Weak Boson Fusion to explore a previously uncharted energy range. Through a simulation using MCGPJ and PYTHIA, we propose designing a weak boson fusion section where a neutral weak boson, emitted by a neutrino, interacts with a charged lepton, resulting in a hadron jet production via a heavy flavor charm or bottom. Given the scarcity of WGCCP events, we suggest enhancing the signal by considering an event where a hadron jet arises from the decay of a heavy flavor charm or bottom produced in a WCPpCCP interaction. To more effectively identify these events, we propose a search strategy that involves detecting a heavy flavor decay, which could manifest as an electron, muon, or jet, in proximity to the hadron jet.

This paper presents the findings of a Godel-variant of a first-order arithmetic system developed by Kleene, in which the fixed-point theorem has been replaced with an explicit proof by Godel. We demonstrate that even without relying on the fixed-point theorem, Godel was still capable of proving arithmetical theorems now commonly attributed to Godel, as well as additional theorems by Kleene, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser that require the diagonalization technique. Furthermore, we show that a similar Godel-style system can also be constructed for a first-order logical system developed by Hilbert and Ackerman, where the fixed-point theorem is again Godel-replaceable, allowing for equivalent proofs of various theorema mentioned earlier, as well as others.

We provide concrete examples demonstrating that in fractional-order dynamical systems defined by $D_t^{\alpha} x_i = f_i(\mathbf{x})$ for $i=1,2$, where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are quadratic polynomials, certain invariant surfaces observed in first-order systems no longer guarantee invariant behavior when $\alpha \neq 1$. This insettedtedted point out that the invariant surface observed in first-order systems may not guarantee invariant behavior when $\alpha \neq 1$.

This study presents experimental results demonstrating how source reconstruction in structural acoustic problems can be significantly improved with pre-existing knowledge, pre-trained models, and advanced optimization strategies. A key obstacle in implementing this technology on a large scale is the computationally intensive nature of obtaining a reliable transfer function for larger structures. However, we were able to overcome this obstacle using an iterative method that involves measuring the structure multiple times with varying speaker-microphone configurations to calculate the transfer function with a single measurement in a subsequent step. Additionally, we showed that source inversion in structural acoustic problems is challenging due to ill-poised issues by investigating the effectiveness of deep learning-based methods in this context. Using a structure with a non-uniform impulse response, we demonstrated how standard source inversion algorithms may yield inaccurate results in structural acoustic problems. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into source inversion and transfer function estimation in structural acoustic problems.
